newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: CZECH-SLOVAK BEER WAR LOOMS AFTER SLOVAK QUOTA.
newsitem.headline: CZECH-SLOVAK BEER WAR LOOMS AFTER SLOVAK QUOTA.

text.p: A beer war between the Czech Republic and Slovakia looms after Bratislava imposed a highly restrictive 532,000 hectolitre annual import quota on Czech beer.
The measure, introduced last week, was justified by Slovak officials and brewers as a "normal" measure to protect a domestic industry finding it dificult to cope with stiff foreign competition.

"The quota should help our brewers fight the ever-growing penetration of Czech breweries in the Slovak market which is increasing year by year," Jozef Hudec of the Slovak Agriculture Ministry told Reuters.
"This is a very common measure to protect domestic producers in many countries," added Stefan Karsay, owner of Slovakia's fourth largest brewer, Pivovar Karsay.

But Czech breweries, which have been aggressively pushing exports at a time when the domestic beer industry is being hit by declining comsumption and low profitability, were both confused and angered.

"We are disappointed by this decision...as our key trademark in Slovakia, Staropramen, competes by quality and not price," Diana Dobalova, spokeswoman for Prazske Pivovary a.s. which is 55-percent owned by Britain's Bass , told Reuters.

Another Czech brewer, Radegast a.s. which is 33 percent owned by Bass, repeated a theme voiced by several Czech breweries polled by Reuters that they did not know how much of their own exports to Slovakia they would be forced to cut.

"Of course we're not pleased by this. We were just told that every (Czech) exporter would receive its own quota for the next period but we still don't know how much it will be," said a Radegast official.
Radegast, the second largest Czech brewer by market share exported 136,000 hectolitres of beer to Slovakia in 1996, out of total exports of 186,000 hectolitres.
The limit figure of 532,000 was arrived at by taking the average level of Czech beer imports over the last three years.
In 1996, the Czechs exported around 643,000 hectolitres of beer to Slovakia after 484,000 in 1995 and 464,000 in 1994
"In the first five months of this year we imported 174,000 hectolitres of Czech beer which was 17.2 percent more than in the same period of 1996," said Hudec.

He added that the quota for each Czech beer would be set every quarter by the Czech Industry Ministry and the Slovak Economy Ministry when regular export-licences are allocated. The next date was set at June 15, he said.
The official Czech reaction to the move was short but succinct. "The beer quota is an unfortunate measure," Czech Industry Minister Karel Kuhnl said in an interview for Czech daily Pravo on Tuesday.
"In our opinion it will have no effect on Slovak breweries as the hole in the market will simply be filled with beer imports from third countries," Kuhnl was quoted as saying.

Slovak breweries, always considered second-rank producers in the federal Czechoslovakia where the market was dominated by world-wide famous Czech trade marks, are plagued by outdated production facilities and a less celebrated brewing tradition.
Unlike the Czech Republic, there are no breweries on the Bratislava Stock Exchange, although Karsay said he would like his brewery to be listed.
Contemplating the effect of the quota, Slovak lovers of Czech beer said they were horrified at the potential consequence of the move.
"I can't imagine offering any Slovak beer to my guests, if I run out of my Budweiser quota by, let's say by November," said the owner of a pub serving the Czech brew in Bratislava.
"Maybe we will just have to smuggle it in, just like in ancient times," another pub owner said.
-- Bratislava Newsroom, 421-7-521-8402
